title: Antigone: family duty vs state law
subtitle: Conscience versus decree
subject: mythologie
description: Antigone buries her brother against the orders of King Creon. Sophocles poses a conflict that is still current: state law or higher moral duty?

hero.hook: A king forbids burying a traitor. A sister disobeys. Two justices clash, and Thebes collapses.

blocks.text: **Antigone** is the daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta. Towards **441 BC B.C.**, the tragedian **Sophocles** made her the heroine of a play that has become universal.

Facing King **Creon**, she asks a question that spans the centuries: when a state law contradicts a higher moral conviction, should we obey or resist? It's not good versus evil here. These are two ideas of justice that collide.

sections.title: Two dead brothers, a cruel decree

blocks.text: In , after the exile of Oedipus, his sons **Eteocle** and **Polyneices** were to reign in turn. Eteocles refuses to give in. Polyneices attacks his own city with a foreign army. The two brothers kill each other. [[Thebes]]

blocks.caption: Antigone facing Creon: family piety against state order.

blocks.text: Creon, their uncle, takes power. Eteocles, defender of the city, will have a solemn funeral. Polyneices, treated as a traitor, will remain unburied. For the Greeks, it is terrifying: without rite, the soul wanders near the , river of the Underworld, without rest. [[Styx]]
A simple handful of earth was enough, symbolically, to complete the funeral rite. Antigone's act is discreet... and fraught with consequences.

Antigone refuses. She does not deny Polyneices' betrayal. It states that no king can cancel the duties owed to the dead. Her sister **Ismène** hesitates, cautious. Antigone acts alone and covers the body.

blocks.caption: Antigone performing the funeral rite for Polyneices.

blocks.text: Before Creon, she claims the : “unwritten and immutable” laws, older than human decrees. Creon sees this as a threat to the State. He condemns her to be walled up alive. [[Natural law]]

**Haemon**, son of Creon and fiancé of Antigone, tries to reason with his father. Creon locks himself away. The soothsayer **Tirésias** announces the anger of the gods: the city is sullied by the abandoned corpse and by the imprisonment of Antigone.

blocks.caption: At the tomb, too late: the tragedy carries away Antigone and Haemon.

blocks.text: Creon finally gives in, too late. Antigone hanged herself. Haemon commits suicide. **Eurydice**, wife of Creon, kills herself. In wanting to save the law, Creon destroyed his family. He remains alone, king of an order that has become empty.

Sophocles does not make Creon a simple villain. He is a leader who wants to avoid chaos. Antigone is extremely rigid. The  sees the collision of two spheres: the family against the city. [[The Hegelian dialectic of Antigone]]
In 1944,  was played during the Occupation. The German censorship saw it as Creon's order; the French public often reads there the heroism of the Resistance. [[Antigone by Jean Anouilh (1944)]]

The conflict between individual conscience and reason of state remains at the heart of political thought. Antigone reminds us that absolute justice, without dialogue, can destroy those it claims to defend.
Antigone opposes the sacred laws of the family to Creon's decree. Their mutual refusal to compromise ruins Thebes and the royal lineage.
